stories.title: AI Is Turning Retail Leasing Into an Underwriting Business
stories.excerpt: Retail real estate has never lacked data. It has lacked a reliable way to connect that data to the health of an individual store. A rent roll shows what a tenant is obligated to pay. Demographics describe the households surrounding a property. Traffic counts estimate the number of cars passing a site. None of those measures, on its own, answers the questions that increasingly matter to shopping center owners and brokers: Is this store productive? Does its customer actually shop this trade area? How does it compare with other locations in the chain? And, if the tenant leaves, who is most likely to replace it successfully? That gap is narrowing. Retail landlords now have access to combinations of mobile location data, credit and debit card transactions, point-of-sale feeds, tenant credit information, and artificial intelligence. The important shift is not simply that more data exists. It is that information, once scattered across spreadsheets, reports and separate platforms, can now increasingly be analyzed together quickly enough to influence a lease, acquisition or merchandising decision. Ashkán Zandieh. PHOTO: Courtesy CRETI Placer.ai helped push location intelligence into the mainstream by allowing owners and brokers to analyze visits, trade areas and cross-shopping. CenterCheck approaches the market from a different angle, using anonymized card transactions to estimate store-level sales. Guesst connects directly with tenant point-of-sale systems to automate sales reporting, while RetailStat combines retailer financial health, credit risk, store locations and market activity. SiteZeus applies AI and predictive modeling to site selection and sales forecasting. Individually, each answers a different question. Together, they are beginning to resemble a retail underwriting stack. For a neighborhood or grocery-anchored shopping center, that changes how a rent roll can be evaluated. bullets: AI and data integration now connect traffic, POS, card transactions to individual store productivity.
Retail landlords can now underwrite tenant quality and replacement likelihood faster than before.
Data consolidation shortens lease, acquisition, and merchandising decision cycles for shopping center owners.
stories.summary: Retail real estate is adopting AI-driven underwriting by combining mobile location data, credit/debit card transactions, POS feeds, and tenant credit information on unified platforms. Previously scattered across spreadsheets, this data can now be analyzed in real time to assess store productivity, customer fit, and competitive positioning across chains. The shift enables landlords and brokers to make faster, more informed decisions on leasing, acquisitions, and tenant replacement.
stories.impact: Faster retail tenant underwriting reduces landlord risk and may stabilize retail property valuations, which indirectly supports mixed-use and retail-anchored multifamily development feasibility. Strong retail anchors (grocery, dining) increasingly depend on data-proven location quality—developers pursuing grocery-anchored mixed-use projects should expect landlords to demand this intelligence, raising due diligence costs and timelines slightly upfront but improving long-term anchor stability.

stories.title: Treasury Yield Curves Split, Raising Questions About What Comes Next for U.S. Economy
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary The Treasury market is delivering an unusually divided assessment of the U.S. economy. The 10-year/2-year spread narrowed to 39 basis points last week, down sharply from 50 basis points a week earlier and approaching its 2026 low of 22 basis points. At the same time, the 10-year/three-month spread stood at 83 basis points, leaving a 44-basis-point gap between the two measures. The divergence reflects dramatically different pricing at the short end of the curve: the two-year Treasury has risen as investors price greater odds of a rate increase, while three-month rates remain closely anchored to the Fed’s current policy setting. Similar disconnects occurred in 1998, 2019 and at the beginning of the 2022-2024 inversion cycle. History suggests the split itself does not predict recession, but it can signal a transition in expectations about monetary policy and growth. Two Curves, Two Economic Messages Developing a clear read on the U.S. economic outlook is challenging these days, a reality underscored by the widening split between two of the Treasury market’s most closely watched yield curves. The 10-year Treasury ended Tuesday at 4.73%, compared with 4.34% for the two-year, producing a 39-basis-point 2s10s spread. The 10-year/three-month spread, however, finished at 83 basis points, according to Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis data. That 44-basis-point difference between the two curve measures is important. It essentially represents the unusually large premium investors are demanding to hold two-year Treasuries rather than three-month securities; a reflection of expectations that monetary policy may become tighter before it becomes easier. The 2s10s spread has flattened substantially since the Iran war began on Feb. 28 and has moved back toward its June low near 22 basis points. bullets: 10-year/2-year Treasury spread narrowed to 39 bps, approaching 22 bps 2026 low.
Two-year yields rising on expected rate increase odds while three-month rates stay anchored to Fed policy.
44 bps gap between two-year/10-year and three-month/10-year spreads signals uncertain monetary policy transition.
stories.summary: The Treasury market is sending mixed signals. The 10-year/2-year spread compressed to 39 basis points last week from 50 bps a week prior, nearing its 2026 low of 22 bps. Meanwhile, the 10-year/three-month spread sits at 83 bps, creating a 44 bp gap that reflects heavy two-year premium pricing on expectations of tighter monetary policy before easing. This divergence occurred similarly in 1998, 2019, and early 2022–2024 but does not itself predict recession.
stories.impact: Curve flattening combined with two-year upward pressure signals uncertainty in refinancing trajectories for floating-rate construction debt and bridge loans. Developers with floating-rate commitments or planned 2027–2028 takeout financing should lock in longer-dated fixed rates now; rising two-year expectations could widen spreads and raise cost of capital for stabilized-asset refinances in late 2026 and 2027.

stories.title: Integral Announces Construction Start for 900-Unit Durham Apartment Development
stories.excerpt: Dubbed Tribute Rising, The Integral Group announced when it will kick off construction on the 907-unit apartment and retail venture. The company anticipates starting construction in early 2027 as the development qualifies for expedited review because the first phase has at least 100 dedicated affordable units. It will also include a grocery store and childcare center. The first phase will deliver in late 2028. The total estimated development cost is $343 million. The first phase will have 332 units with a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom units. Phase two will have 250 units and phase three will have 325 units. The Triangle Business Journal reports that Integral was chosen by the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) for the 15-acre redevelopment of the Forest Hills Heights public housing community on West Lakewood Avenue. Anticipated funding so far includes $19 million from DHA, $19 million in equity and an $80 million loan.  The post Integral Announces Construction Start for 900-Unit Durham Apartment Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Integral Group: 907-unit Tribute Rising in Durham, NC; $343M total dev cost, phases 2027–2029.
First phase: 332 units with 100+ affordable units, grocery, childcare; $80M loan + $19M DHA + $19M equity.
Expedited review granted due to affordable housing component; first delivery Q4 2028.
stories.summary: Integral Group announced construction start in early 2027 for Tribute Rising, a 907-unit mixed-use development in Durham, NC redeveloping the Forest Hills Heights public housing community. Phase one (332 units, late 2028 delivery) qualifies for expedited permitting via 100+ dedicated affordable units and adds grocery and childcare. Total project cost is $343 million, funded by $80 million debt, $19 million DHA contribution, and $19 million equity. Phase two and three add 250 and 325 units respectively.
stories.impact: Durham's affordability inclusion and public-housing redevelopment signal strong municipal demand-pull and pipeline confidence. The phased 2027–2029 delivery into a Raleigh-Durham market with robust tech employment (Oracle, Apple, Meta presence) positions affordable-skewing units to absorb strong renter demand. Developers should monitor Durham entitlement timeline as a model for expedited affordable review nationally and watch for competing supply as other developers chase same demand tailwinds.

stories.title: Related Pays $110M for Atlanta-Area Apartments
stories.excerpt: Related Company paid $110 million for a 468-unit garden-style apartment complex the Roswell/Alpharetta area. The seller was Post Real Estate Group. The Manchester at Mansell apartments were built in 1984 and offer one-, two-, and three-bedroom floor plans. Manchester at Mansell has rental units ranging from 857 to 1,540 square feet, starting at $1,330. Amenities include a pool, fitness center, clubhouse and tennis court. That Atlanta Business Chronicle reports the asset last exchanged hands in 2018 when the Post Investment Group bought it for $72.5 million. Post Real Estate Group, an operating subsidiary of Post Investment Group, still owns a handful of multifamily properties in the area, comprising just over 2,600 residential units. Founded in 2007 and headquartered in Beverly Hills, CA, the company operates in more than 20 states and encompasses the following industries: real estate investments, real estate services, insurance, consumer goods, manufacturing, consumer services, and franchising. The post Related Pays $110M for Atlanta-Area Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Related Co. paid $110M for 468-unit Manchester at Mansell, Roswell/Alpharetta, Georgia.
Asset last traded 2018 at $72.5M; current rents $1,330+; built 1984, garden-style.
Price implies ~51% appreciation over 6 years; seller Post RE Group retains 2,600+ units in region.
stories.summary: Related Company acquired the Manchester at Mansell, a 468-unit 1984-vintage garden-style complex in the Roswell/Alpharetta submarket north of Atlanta, for $110 million. The asset last sold in 2018 to Post Investment Group for $72.5 million, representing 51% appreciation. Units range from 857 to 1,540 SF at rents starting at $1,330. Related's purchase signals confidence in the North Atlanta corridor despite the vintage and market competition.
stories.impact: North Atlanta (Roswell/Alpharetta/Sandy Springs) remains a high-demand infill submarket for institutional capital; Related's aggressive repricing of aging garden-stock reflects strong rent growth and yield compression. For Trammell Crow and peer developers, this signals that even 40+ year-old assets command robust valuations in prime North Atlanta corridors—new supply here must command significant rent premiums to justify construction costs, or developers should focus on underserved suburban rings farther north and east to avoid direct competition with trophy-asset prices.

stories.title: Manhattan Housing Seasonality: When the Borough Sees its Peaks and Valleys
stories.excerpt: School calendars, holidays and even the weather can all have an impact on housing market activity across the borough of Manhattan. So can assumptions from buyers when it comes to the strength of the spring and fall markets. The months of March, April, May, June and October have historically — at least from 2015 through 2025 — been the most active months for sales of condos and co-ops in Manhattan, with the average number of sales typically climbing over 1,000 per month, according to the latest data from Corcoran Sunshine, shared exclusively with Commercial Observer. General seasonal drivers of the Manhattan housing market include the school year calendar, which determines when moves to new homes will be least disruptive. Another factor is the timing of corporate bonuses, which tend to arrive between January and March. Meanwhile, family vacations, back-to-school transitions, Labor Day weekend and religious holidays can all contribute to a general market lull. However, sales tend to climb back up after September alongside normalizing schedules, an influx of listings, cooler weather and looming year-end tax implications. From January to July 2026, a total of 7,239 condo and co-op sales closed in Manhattan, with over 1,000 each in March, April, May and June, according to the Corcoran Sunshine analysis. Historically, the most listings have been in September, with the average number that month hitting 2,264 between 2016 and 2025, while December saw the lowest number of new listings with 730. GRAPH: Cocoran Sunshine Meanwhile, the numbers for condos and co-ops above $5 million looked a little different this year compared to the average. From January to July 2026, the number of sales of condos and co-ops over $5 million totaled 576, while the average amount of sales during that time from 2016 through 2025 was 495, according to the data. The higher numbers for this year come in the aftermath of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-a-terre tax, which imposes an annual property tax sur
bullets: Manhattan condo/co-op sales peak March–June and October; average >1,000 sales/month historically.
School calendars, corporate bonuses (Jan–Mar), family vacations, and year-end tax implications drive seasonality.
September sees post-summer rebound: new listings, cooler weather, back-to-school transitions normalize activity.
stories.summary: Manhattan residential sales follow a strong seasonal pattern. Peak activity occurs in March, April, May, June, and October, each averaging over 1,000 sales per month from 2015–2025 data. School calendars, January-to-March corporate bonuses, family vacation timing, and year-end tax deadlines all influence activity. Summer and early fall typically see lower volume; activity rebounds sharply in September as schedules normalize, listings increase, and tax-year deadlines approach.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily developers; Manhattan condo/co-op seasonality is distinct from rental-market dynamics and does not materially signal apartment demand trends. Apartment renters are less bound by school calendars and tax timing than condo buyers. However, developers of mixed-use or condo-rental projects in Manhattan should note that September–October windows are optimal for pre-lease and lease-up activity given buyer/renter appetite surges.

stories.title: Shoma Group Obtains $172.5M C-PACE Loan for North Bay Village Development
stories.excerpt: Newmark has arranged $172.5 million in C-PACE construction financing on behalf of Shoma Group for Shoma Bay, a landmark mixed-use waterfront development in North Bay Village, Florida. Located at 1850 John F. Kennedy Causeway, the 24-story development will comprise 333 luxury condominium residences and a retail component anchored by a new 36,000-square-foot Publix Super Market. Newmark’s Anthony Orso, Clifford Welden, Daniel Matz and Henry Stimler arranged the financing on behalf of Shoma Group. The financing was provided by Nuveen Green Capital, led by Christopher Lawton, Ryan Doyle, Brendan Moore and Tyler Amano. Shoma Bay will feature 333 luxury residences, ranging from studios to three-bedroom condominiums and penthouses. The development will offer more than 60,000 square feet of amenities, including a rooftop pool deck, zen garden, wellness spa with hammam, two-story fitness center, padel court, owners’ lounge and business and co-working spaces. Shoma Bay will also feature a retail promenade anchored by Publix, complemented by additional dining and retail offerings. The post Shoma Group Obtains $172.5M C-PACE Loan for North Bay Village Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Shoma Group: $172.5M C-PACE financing for Shoma Bay, North Bay Village, Florida mixed-use waterfront.
333 luxury condos (studios–3BR penthouses) + 36,000 SF Publix anchor; 24 stories, 60,000 SF amenities.
Nuveen Green Capital provided C-PACE; Newmark arranged; development on Kennedy Causeway waterfront.
stories.summary: Shoma Group secured $172.5 million in C-PACE construction financing via Nuveen Green Capital (arranged by Newmark) for Shoma Bay, a 24-story mixed-use waterfront tower in North Bay Village, Florida. The development comprises 333 luxury residences (studios through penthouse), 36,000 SF Publix anchor, and 60,000 SF of amenities including rooftop pools, spa, fitness, and co-working. C-PACE structures offer lower cost of capital than standard commercial financing.
stories.impact: C-PACE financing for luxury condo (not multifamily rental) has limited direct bearing on apartment development. However, Shoma Bay signals that South Florida waterfront development remains well-capitalized and that green-focused capital (Nuveen) is active. For multifamily developers, this underscores South Florida market strength but also rising construction costs for premium waterfront—developers should lock land positions in secondary corridors (Wynwood, Allapattah, Aventura) to capture spillover rental demand at more feasible rents.

stories.title: Trammell Crow Company Breaks Ground on Hillsboro Industrial Park
stories.excerpt: Trammell Crow Company (TCC) has broken ground on Phase II of Sewell Corporate Park in Hillsboro, Oregon, approximately 20 miles west of Portland. Phase II, located on 17.76 acres, will include two speculative buildings totaling 294,700 square feet. The groundbreaking of Phase II comes less than a year after Phase I delivered two buildings totaling 396,212 square feet. Clayton Madey of Macadam Forbes is marketing the three remaining buildings for sale or for lease. “We remain the most active developer in Hillsboro and in the Sunset Corridor with the recent groundbreaking of phase two of Sewell Corporate Park, a development focused on serving the needs of west side high tech businesses and the companies that serve them,” said Steve Sieber, a principal with TCC in Portland. Phase II of Sewell Corporate Park was designed by MDG Architecture and is being built by Perlo Construction. TCC is also underway with VanRose Technology Center, a 303,969-square-foot logistics building. The post Trammell Crow Company Breaks Ground on Hillsboro Industrial Park appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: TCC breaks ground Phase II Sewell Corporate Park, Hillsboro, OR (west of Portland); 17.76 acres.
Phase II: 294,700 SF spec industrial across two buildings; Phase I delivered 396,212 SF in <1 year.
TCC also underway on VanRose Technology Center, 303,969 SF logistics; serves west-side high-tech firms.
stories.summary: Trammell Crow Company broke ground on Phase II of Sewell Corporate Park near Hillsboro, Oregon, 20 miles west of Portland. The phase spans 17.76 acres and includes two speculative industrial buildings totaling 294,700 SF. Phase I, completed less than a year ago, delivered 396,212 SF across two buildings. TCC is also constructing VanRose Technology Center (304k SF logistics) nearby to serve the region's high-tech and semiconductor supply-chain ecosystem.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily; industrial development and tech-corridor logistics do not drive apartment demand in the same submarket. However, TCC's aggressive industrial expansion in the Sunset Corridor (Hillsboro) near Intel, Taiwan Semiconductor, and other chipmakers signals sustained high-wage tech employment. For multifamily developers targeting Portland suburbs, Hillsboro/Beaverton remain strong employment anchors—consider multifamily development south and east of TCC's industrial holdings to capture worker demand while avoiding land-cost inflation around TCC's logistics corridor.

stories.title: Robert Milne of Prospect Ridge: 5 Questions

The credit vehicle was rolled out on the heels of Prospect Ridge’s debut $500 million fund that focused heavily on transitional and value-add opportunities. Robert Milne, managing director and co-head of credit strategies at Prospect Ridge, spoke with Commercial Observer about the goals behind the new fund, deployment plans and how the overall CRE debt markets are shaping up for the rest of 2026. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What was the impetus for launching this second fund? Robert Milne: We think there’s a great opportunity in the debt markets right now, coming off of the interest rate increases and what’s happened to valuations across a lot of sectors. We think we’re lending against reset valuations in most sectors. We are lending well below replacement cost, but at the same time fundamentals in the sector we’re lending against are very strong. We’re seeing underlying rent growth and strong occupancies. We think we’re at a great point in the market and we’re going to be able to invest the fund well. Describe what deployment is typically like for Prospect Ridge credit vehicles? The first fund is fully fully deployed and almost fully realized. We were generally targeting institutional borrowers who have business plans that we believe in. They tend to be on the larger end of loans. We target $65 million to $300 million whole loans. bullets: Prospect Ridge closes $800M Fund II with $3B total lending capacity; first fund was $500M.
Provides first-mortgage, mezzanine, preferred equity across US sectors; debt market favorable post-rate increases.
Focus on transitional and value-add CRE opportunities as valuations have reset materially.
stories.summary: Prospect Ridge Real Estate Debt Fund II closed with $800 million in capital commitments and $3 billion total lending capacity, following its debut $500 million fund. The vehicle deploys first mortgages, mezzanine loans, and preferred equity across all property types in the U.S. Managing director Robert Milne attributed strong investor appetite to favorable debt market timing following recent rate increases and valuation resets, with particular focus on transitional and value-add opportunities.
stories.impact: Growing non-bank debt capacity signals improved financing availability for development and value-add across sectors, including multifamily. Reset valuations post-rate hikes mean acquisition pricing has rationalized; developers with development-stage projects and value-add portfolios can now find constructive lenders at more reasonable leverage. However, competition for deals is intensifying as capital floods the space—lock land and pre-lease early to command better terms and execution timelines.

stories.title: The Plan: At 44 West Eighth Street, the Goal Is a ‘Wonderful Visual Cacophony’
stories.excerpt: Craftsmen often like to leave a bit of themselves behind in the things they create, and that is especially true at 44 West Eighth Street, a new ground-up condominium development in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The exterior facade is made from handmade Petersen brick, which is sourced from Denmark, and each brick bears the thumbmarks of its maker. The brickmakers have for over 200 years used this method of hand-pressing the bricks in a wooden mold, then pushing them out, leaving a pair of thumbprints, according to developer T30 Capital and designer Idan Naor of InWorkshop. The minds behind 44 West Eighth Street wanted to create something unique, holistic and human that honors the area’s historic significance, while bringing a modern development to the neighborhood of narrow streets and sometimes narrower buildings. “This spot is totally irresistible for condos, mostly because of the width,” Margaret Grossman, co-founder and managing partner at T30 Capital, told Commercial Observer. “It’s 50 feet wide, and it is so rare to be able to build a new building in Greenwich Village with that width. It’s double the width of a townhouse you could get here; even the very few condos that have been built here can’t offer that. We just knew that we could create these exceptionally special, very gracious condominiums with really spectacular proportions.” There will be a total of five residences in the building, and a substantial portion of the construction is expected to be completed either late this year or early next year. The certificate of occupancy and closings are expected in the late spring or early summer of 2027. bullets: 44 West 8th Street, NYC: five luxury residences; hand-pressed Danish Petersen brick facade.
Prices $9.75M–$20M full-floor to penthouse; developer T30 Capital; rooftop terrace, gym, sauna.
Ultra-luxury micro-building in Greenwich Village; architectural distinction via handmade materials and design.
stories.summary: T30 Capital is developing 44 West 8th Street in Manhattan's Greenwich Village as a five-unit luxury residential micro-building. Each residence features handmade Danish Petersen brick with maker's thumbprints, with pricing from $9.75 million (full-floor) to $20 million (penthouse). Amenities include private penthouse rooftop terrace, lower-level gym, and sauna. The design emphasizes artisanal materials and human-scale craftsmanship in a historically significant neighborhood.
stories.impact: No direct relevance to multifamily apartment development. Ultra-luxury condo boutique projects in prime Manhattan operate in a distinct capital and buyer-profile universe from rental apartments. However, the project signals that Greenwich Village—traditionally renter-dense and high-rent—is still attracting trophy capital for ownership-product conversions; multifamily developers should monitor if more such conversions accelerate, potentially tightening rental supply in the submarket and supporting rate growth in competing rental buildings nearby.

stories.title: Tax-Exempt Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities Are Having a Moment
stories.excerpt: As the need for affordable housing in the U.S. grows, the tax-exempt commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) market is emerging as a potential financing tool to deliver more homes. New federal rules and greater attention from ratings agencies and top-tier banks are helping the growth of the burgeoning structure. Tax-exempt affordable housing securitizations have taken flight of late after years of largely flying under the radar, according to Ryan Paszczykowski, head of structured investing at Systima Capital Management. Tax-exempt CMBS deals occurred on an occasional basis back in the 2000s, but the structure began to develop consistently in the late 2010s when Citigroup and Freddie Mac rolled out programs offering credit risk transfer securities backed by tax-exempt loans issued by state or local housing agencies. The tax-exempt structures of these deals offer lower costs of capital than standard taxable CMBS or traditional affordable housing loans backed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. Freddie Mac then launched a multifamily loan program in 2017 securitized by tax-exempt loans tied to properties receiving new-issue 4 percent Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) and expanded its outreach of the offering in late 2024 through a new registration system. Now, the product is starting to take hold as a securitized offering in the municipal debt space at a time when there is increased support nationally to find financial solutions for America’s housing challenges. The deals have become more attractive to investors in a higher interest rate climate since the value of tax-exempt debt stays higher as rates remain elevated while also serving as an attractive option for high-yield investors who are drawn to collateral protections like the federally backed LIHTCs. A recent deal that Systima itself was involved in underscores the increased demand. bullets: Tax-exempt CMBS market emerging for affordable housing; Citigroup/Freddie Mac programs launched late 2010s.
Freddie Mac added multifamily securitization program in 2017 tied to 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit deals.
Tax-exempt structures offer lower cost of capital than taxable CMBS or traditional Fannie/Freddie affordable loans.
stories.summary: Tax-exempt commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) are gaining traction as a financing tool for affordable housing. While occasional in the 2000s, the structure matured consistently in the late 2010s via Citigroup and Freddie Mac credit-risk-transfer programs backing tax-exempt loans from state/local housing agencies. Freddie Mac expanded into multifamily securitization in 2017 with products linked to 4% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit properties. Tax-exempt structures reduce capital costs relative to taxable CMBS or traditional GSE affordable loans.
stories.impact: Tax-exempt CMBS provides materially cheaper financing for LIHTC-eligible multifamily projects (typically capped at 60% AMI). For developers pursuing mixed-income or affordable-anchored developments, tax-exempt securitization now rivals or beats traditional LIHTC-stacked financing on cost and simplifies capital structures. Expect increased competition for LIHTC allocations as this capital becomes more available; lock in state allocation timelines and develop LIHTC applications earlier in underwriting cycles to secure financing commitments.
